title: 8.01 Lecture 1 — Units, Dimensions & Powers of Ten
text: Any measurement you make without knowledge of its uncertainty is meaningless. In physics we express every quantity in SI units: the meter for length, the kilogram for mass, the second for time. Dimensional analysis is a powerful check: the dimensions on the left of an equation must equal the dimensions on the right, or the equation is wrong. If a result for a length comes out with dimensions of time, you have made a mistake.

title: 8.01 Lecture 2 — One-Dimensional Kinematics
text: Velocity is the rate of change of position with time, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time. Average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time, while instantaneous velocity is the slope of the position-time curve at an instant. An object can have zero velocity yet non-zero acceleration: at the top of its flight a ball thrown straight up is momentarily at rest, but gravity still accelerates it downward at 9.8 meters per second squared.

title: 8.01 Lecture 3 — Vectors & Projectile Motion
text: The great insight of projectile motion is that the horizontal and vertical motions are completely independent. Gravity acts only vertically, so the horizontal velocity is constant while the vertical velocity changes at 9.8 meters per second squared. Because the two are independent, a bullet fired horizontally and a bullet dropped from the same height hit the ground at the same time. The trajectory traced out is a parabola. Vectors are decomposed into perpendicular components to analyze such motion.

title: 8.01 Lecture 4 — Newton's Laws of Motion
text: Newton's first law says an object stays at rest, or moves at constant velocity, unless a net force acts on it; this is inertia. The second law makes it quantitative: the net force equals mass times acceleration, F equals m a. The third law says that if body A pushes on body B, then B pushes back on A with equal magnitude and opposite direction. These action and reaction forces act on different objects, which is why they never cancel. A free-body diagram isolates the forces on one object.

title: 8.01 Lecture 5 — Uniform Circular Motion
text: An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating, because the direction of its velocity is always changing. That acceleration points toward the center of the circle and is called centripetal acceleration; its magnitude is v squared divided by r. There is no such thing as centrifugal force pushing you outward. What you feel is your own inertia, and some real force such as tension, friction, or gravity must point inward to keep you on the circular path.

title: 8.01 Lecture 6 — Friction
text: Friction opposes relative motion between surfaces. The maximum static friction force is the coefficient of static friction times the normal force, and once sliding begins the kinetic friction force is the coefficient of kinetic friction times the normal force. Kinetic friction is generally weaker than the maximum static friction. Friction does not depend on the contact area, only on the normal force pressing the surfaces together and the nature of the materials.

title: 8.01 Lecture 7 — Work, Energy & the Work-Energy Theorem
text: Work is force times displacement in the direction of the force. The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy, one half m v squared. Energy is conserved: it changes form between kinetic and potential but is never created or destroyed. Gravitational potential energy near Earth is m g h, and as an object falls that potential energy converts into kinetic energy.

title: 8.01 Lecture 8 — Momentum & Collisions
text: Momentum is mass times velocity, and the total momentum of a closed system is conserved when no external force acts. In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved; in an inelastic collision momentum is conserved but some kinetic energy is lost to heat and deformation. Impulse, the force applied over a time interval, equals the change in momentum. This is why airbags and crumple zones extend the collision time to reduce the force.

title: 8.01 Lecture 9 — Universal Gravitation
text: Newton's law of universal gravitation says every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The same force that makes an apple fall keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth. The gravitational acceleration g at Earth's surface is about 9.8 meters per second squared, and it decreases with the square of the distance from the center of the Earth.

title: 8.01 Lecture 10 — Simple Harmonic Motion
text: When a restoring force is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium, the result is simple harmonic motion, as with a mass on a spring or a small-angle pendulum. The motion is sinusoidal in time, characterized by its amplitude, period, and frequency. For a spring the period depends on the mass and the spring constant; for a pendulum the period depends on the length and the gravitational acceleration, but not on the mass or, for small swings, the amplitude.
